title: How a car works
summary: Follow the push inside a petrol car, from burning fuel all the way to spinning wheels.
objective: Explain how burning fuel in the engine ends up turning a car's wheels.

hook.prompt: In a petrol car, what actually makes the car move forward?

options.text: Burning fuel pushing on parts inside the engine
A big battery spinning a motor
options.feedback: That's how electric cars work. A petrol car gets its push from burning its fuel.

options.text: Exhaust gas blasting out of the back pipe, like a rocket
options.feedback: The exhaust pipe only carries used gas away. It doesn't push the car along.

options.text: Air rushing in through the front of the car
options.feedback: Air does go into the engine, but on its own it can't push anything. It needs fuel to burn with.

hook.explanation: Tiny fires inside the engine do the pushing, many times a second. Let's see how that push ends up turning the wheels.

bricks.title: Fuel burns and pushes a piston
bricks.body: Most cars burn **petrol** or diesel. Fuel stores lots of energy, and the engine's job is to let it out. Inside the engine are strong metal tubes called **cylinders**. In each one, a little air and fuel are set alight. They burn so fast it's like a tiny explosion, and the hot gas shoves a sliding plug, the **piston**, down the tube. (Electric cars work differently, with a battery and a motor.)

term.definition: A metal plug that slides up and down inside a cylinder, shoved by burning fuel.

bricks.prompt: A petrol car runs out of fuel and rolls to a stop. Why does the engine stop working?

options.text: There's nothing left to burn, so nothing shoves the pistons
The empty tank makes the car too light to grip the road
options.feedback: An empty tank is only a little lighter. The real problem is that with no fuel, nothing burns, so there's no push.
A petrol car's pushing power doesn't come from a battery. It comes from fuel burning in the cylinders.

bricks.hint: Where does the push on the pistons come from?
bricks.explanation: The push comes from burning fuel. With an empty tank there's nothing to burn in the cylinders, so the pistons stop getting shoved.

bricks.prompt: Tap the part that gets shoved down when the fuel burns.
bricks.hint: Look for the part that can slide along the tube.
bricks.explanation: The blue block is the **piston**. Hot gas from the burning fuel above it shoves it down the cylinder.

bricks.title: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow
bricks.body: Each piston repeats four moves, called **strokes**, many times a second. People remember them as **suck, squeeze, bang, blow**. Suck: the piston slides down and pulls in air and fuel. Squeeze: it slides up and squashes them small. Bang: the **spark plug** makes a spark, the mix burns, and the piston is shoved down. Blow: it slides up and pushes the used gas out to the exhaust pipe.

term.definition: A part at the top of the cylinder that makes a tiny electric spark to light the fuel.

bricks.prompt: Put the piston's four strokes in order.

items.text: The piston slides down, pulling in air and fuel
The piston slides up, squashing the mix
A spark lights the mix and the piston is shoved down
The piston slides up, pushing used gas out

bricks.hint: Air and fuel have to get into the cylinder before they can burn.
bricks.explanation: Air and fuel must get in, be squashed, burn, then leave, which makes room for fresh air and fuel on the next turn.

bricks.prompt: Which stroke does this picture show?

visual.html: Piston moving ↑
visual.alt: A cylinder with the piston moving up near the top, grey gas puffing out of the top, and no spark at the spark plug.

options.feedback: In Suck the piston slides down and air and fuel come in. Here the piston is going up and gas is going out.
In Squeeze the piston also moves up, but the mix stays trapped inside to be squashed. Here gas is leaving the cylinder.
In Bang a spark fires and the piston is shoved down. Here there's no spark and the piston is rising.

bricks.hint: Is gas coming in, staying trapped, or going out?
bricks.explanation: The piston is rising and grey used gas is leaving. That's **Blow**, clearing the cylinder for the next Suck.

bricks.title: From up-and-down to round and round
bricks.body: Pistons only move up and down, but wheels need to spin. Each piston is joined to the **crankshaft**, which turns the up-and-down push into spinning, just like your legs turn bike pedals round. That spin goes through the **gearbox** to the wheels. Low gears give lots of pushing power for starting off and climbing hills. High gears let the wheels spin fast for cruising, like the gears on a bike.

term.definition: A bent rod that turns the pistons' up-and-down pushes into spinning.

bricks.prompt: A car is pulling away up a steep hill. Which gear helps most?

options.feedback: High gears are for spinning the wheels fast when cruising. On a steep hill they don't give enough pushing power.

options.text: Any gear; it makes no difference
options.feedback: Gears change the balance between pushing power and speed, just like on a bike, so the choice matters a lot on a hill.

bricks.hint: Which bike gear would you pick to ride up a hill?
bricks.explanation: Low gears give the wheels lots of pushing power but less speed. Starting up a steep hill needs plenty of push and very little speed.

bricks.prompt: Put the journey of the push in order, from fuel to road.

items.text: The gearbox passes the spin on

bricks.hint: Start where the energy is stored.
bricks.explanation: Burning fuel shoves the piston, the crankshaft turns that push into spin, and the gearbox hands the spin to the wheels.

challenge.prompt: A car's spark plugs stop making sparks, but its tank is full of petrol. What happens?

options.text: No bang, so the pistons aren't shoved and the wheels stop being turned
The fuel still burns, just more slowly
options.feedback: The air and fuel need the spark to start burning. Without it, the Bang stroke never happens.

options.text: Switching to a low gear keeps the car going
options.feedback: Gears only pass on the spin the engine makes. With no bang, there's no spin to pass on.

options.text: The car keeps going, because the full tank still has energy
options.feedback: The energy is there, but it stays locked in the fuel until a spark lets it out by burning it.

challenge.hint: Which of the four strokes needs the spark?
challenge.explanation: The spark starts the burning. No spark means no bang, no push on the pistons, no spinning crankshaft, and nothing for the gearbox to send to the wheels.

takeaways: A petrol engine lets out the energy stored in fuel by burning it inside cylinders.
Each piston repeats suck, squeeze, bang, blow, and the bang is what shoves it.
The crankshaft turns the pistons' push into spin, and the gearbox sends it to the wheels.
Low gears give pushing power for hills and starts; high gears give speed.
